one_liner: Portable, dependency-free C WebAssembly interpreter; fastest of seven interpreters on scalar MVP code, about 1.6x WAMR fast-interp on Apple M4.
what_it_does: Embeddable Wasm runtime in about a dozen C99 source files: m3_NewEnvironment / m3_NewRuntime(stack bytes) / m3_ParseModule / m3_LoadModule, link host functions with m3_LinkRawFunction, then m3_FindFunction and m3_Call or m3_CallV. Functions are compiled lazily into M3 'meta-machine' code on first lookup or call, and the new validator runs as part of that compile. It is its own C API (bindings exist for Rust, Python, Go, Zig, Swift and others), not a drop-in for WAMR's wasm_export.h or Wasmtime's API.
how_it_is_fast: Wasm stack bytecode is translated into 'operations' that are C functions sharing one fixed signature (pc, sp, mem, r0, fp0); each ends by tail-calling the next, so the virtual registers stay in machine registers and there is no central dispatch loop (continuation-passing threaded code, enforced with musttail where the compiler supports it). The compile pass maps the stack machine onto a register-file layout with up to three operation variants per opcode by operand placement, and fuses common sequences. HEAD (after the measured v0.9.0) adds the preserve_none calling convention on x86-64 and AArch64 and fold/fuse passes (set_local folding, compare+branch fusion) that the v0.9.1-beta.1 notes credit with 10-50% speedups on many workloads.
when_to_use: You cannot generate native code (iOS/App Store, watchOS, W^X targets, Wasm-in-Wasm) and the guest is scalar MVP code: on M4 E-cores it was fastest on 14 of the 17 shared cases and within 5% on the other three, including xmrsplayer audio (6.9 ms vs WAMR 11.9 ms and Pulley 15.7 ms per call) and AssemblyScript graphql.
Dispatch-heavy guests (call_indirect, vtable-style polymorphism): 11.7 ms vs WAMR 18.5 ms and Pulley 31.5 ms per call_indirect run on M4.
Microcontrollers and small SoCs (ESP32, nRF52, Cortex-M3/M4/M7, RISC-V, Xtensa, AVR): the README cites about 64 KB of code and 10 KB of RAM as the minimum useful system.
Plugin or scripting hosts that want a C99 library that builds in seconds with no dependencies, plus gas metering, resource caps and suspend/resume snapshots (HEAD).

Short-lived modules where Cranelift compile time would dominate: in wasmi-benchmarks on an EPYC 7763 its lazy-compile startup geomean is 2.77x the fastest versus 56.73x for WAMR fast-interp and 1634x for Wasmtime Cranelift (eager wasm3 is 51.60x, so the win comes from deferring compilation).
when_not_to_use: Peak throughput where a JIT or AOT is allowed: in wasmi-benchmarks on x86-64 it executes at 16.51x the fastest runtime against 1.15x for Wasmtime Cranelift and 1.05x for V8.

SIMD-128 or relaxed-SIMD guests: there is no fixed-width SIMD at all (README lists it N/A), so auto-vectorised builds fail to load; WAMR leads those rows. GC and the full threads proposal are also N/A.

Hosts that instantiate the same module many times: an IM3Module is consumed by the runtime it is loaded into and cannot be cloned (open issue #366), so each fresh instance re-parses and re-validates; extended-const instantiation cost 116-122x Pulley's time on M4.

Assuming the A-tier lead holds on x86-64: in wasmi-benchmarks (EPYC 7763, the same wasm3 v0.9.0 via the wasm3x 0.2.1 crate) it executes at 16.51x the fastest, level with WAMR fast-interp (17.07x) and behind wasmz (15.89x), Stitch (15.73x), Wasmi v2 (12.40x) and Silverfir-nano's interpreter (9.02x).
Teams that need a steady release cadence: v0.5.0 (2021) was the only release until v0.9.0 in August 2026, and the README still declares a minimal maintenance phase.

integration.form: static lib via CMake, or source-drop (compile source/*.c directly; the benchmark built 12 files with clang -c and ar)
integration.dependencies: none for the core; uvwasi or the built-in simple WASI layer optional for WASI
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler (Clang, GCC, MSVC, MinGW-w64, TinyCC, Zig, cosmocc); CMake 3.11+ for the CMake build; guaranteed tail-call dispatch needs a compiler with musttail (Clang, GCC 15)
integration.platforms: x86, x86-64, ARM, AArch64, RISC-V, PowerPC, MIPS, Xtensa, ARC32, AVR; Linux, Windows, macOS, FreeBSD, Android, iOS, OpenWrt, Arduino/PlatformIO/ESP-IDF MCUs, browsers (compiled to Wasm); big-endian supported
integration.thread_safety: Not documented in wasm3.h. Threads are listed N/A; atomics (added 2026-09-29) keep single-thread semantics, and sharing a memory between runtimes needs the separate d_m3HasThreads build option (m3_config.h).

gotchas: Harness asymmetry behind the 'instantiation is its weak spot' figures: for the extended-const rows the benchmark times m3_NewRuntime + m3_ParseModule + m3_LoadModule + m3_FindFunction (lazy compile) + call per sample for wasm3, but only Store + Instance::new + call on a module compiled once for Pulley and WAMR (wasm3.rs vs lib.rs/wamr.rs). wasm3's API forces the re-parse, so the cost is real for users, but the 116-122x compares parse+validate+instantiate against instantiate only. The 17-case execution geomean is unaffected (load and compile are outside the timed window there).

The measured build is v0.9.0 (2026-08-24). HEAD changed the public API: m3_GetMemory and m3_GetMemorySize now take an IM3Module and size_t sizes instead of an IM3Runtime and uint32_t, so v0.9.0 bindings (including the benchmark's own) need updating; HEAD's exception handling, multi-memory, memory64 and atomics are not in v0.9.0, which failed those smoke tests.

Exception handling on HEAD has a documented lifetime hole: exception objects belong to the runtime and are released when the outermost m3_Call returns, so an exnref parked in a global or table 'outlives that and dangles' (m3_config.h).

Security history: several CVEs against v0.5.0, the only release from 2021 to 2026 (heap overflows in m3_compile.c DeallocateSlot, NewCodePage, op_Const64; CVSS up to 9.8; search snippets, NVD pages not opened). v0.9.0 adds full module validation and OSS-Fuzz fixes, so avoid distro or crate packages still pinned to 0.5.0 for untrusted modules.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick wasm3 over WAMR fast-interp and wasmz for scalar MVP guests on Apple Silicon (1.01 vs 1.63 and 1.59 geomean on M4) or when you want the smallest C dependency; pick WAMR when the guest needs SIMD or an AOT/JIT tier later. For Rust hosts on x86-64, Wasmi v2 and Silverfir-nano executed faster in wasmi-benchmarks (12.40 and 9.02 vs 16.51).
verified_claims_summary: In the independent rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark run of 2026-09-22, unpatched wasm3 v0.9.0 (Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12) took 1.01x the fastest runtime's CPU time per call versus 1.63x for WAMR fast-interp and 2.09x for Wasmtime v49 Pulley, geomean over 17 MVP/scalar cases on M4 Max E-cores (1.04 vs 1.38 vs 1.68 on an iPhone XS A12), N=10, results checked against a cross-runtime consensus; I recomputed the Pulley and WAMR M4 geomeans from the per-case table. The competing WAMR, WasmEdge and Pulley builds carried 29, 26 and 9 patches, while wasm3 ran stock.
status_note: Active again in 2026 (v0.9.0 2026-08-24, v0.9.1-beta.1 2026-09-10, last commit 2026-09-29) though the README still says minimal maintenance; MIT-licensed, dependency-free C99 and easy to vendor, with no published GitHub security advisories or SECURITY.md.
